title: Eight Weeks of Beginnings
subtitle: An eight week plan from James Bell for the brand new Christian. What just happened, reading Mark, the prayer Jesus taught, a church and baptism, and the doubts that come, in plain words.
intro:
This is an eight week walk for the brand new Christian, the person something real has just happened to, maybe last night, maybe slowly over months, and who wasn't handed a manual. It uses plain words, and when an old church word can't be avoided, it's explained on the spot. Each week holds one focus, one small daily practice, one thing to read, one tool, and one honest question. The weeks cover what happened to you, reading Mark, praying the prayer Jesus taught, finding a church and asking about baptism, the old habits and the doubts that come back, one friend to walk with, and a few practices to keep for the long road.

It is not a substitute for a pastor, a church, or the people who will walk with you, and if your faith came in the middle of a crisis, it doesn't replace your doctor, your counselor, or your recovery meetings either. If you have thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 now, or 911 if you're in danger. Walk it imperfectly. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up where you stopped. You didn't earn your way into this faith, and you won't be graded on how fast you learn. It runs on grace, God's kindness to people who could never earn it.
careNote: If your faith came in the middle of a crisis, keep seeing your doctor or counselor, and don't stop a medication without your doctor. A church or leader that tries to control your money, your family, or your questions is spiritual abuse, and you can walk away; if someone at home threatens you, Find Help lists who to call, and in a crisis, call or text 988.

weeks.why: People come to faith by different roads. Some can name the night; others only know that somewhere along the way they came to believe Jesus is who he said he was, and told him so. You may feel joy, or relief, or not much at all, and any of those can be the start of real faith, because Christianity doesn't rest on the feeling. When Paul summed up the faith for the church in Corinth, he listed events: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). What happened to you is what Christians call grace, and what comes next is discipleship, learning to live as a student of Jesus, slowly, over years.
weeks.practice: Each day, write two or three sentences about what happened to you and what you notice changing, or not changing. Use your own words rather than borrowed ones, and don't worry about getting the vocabulary right. Nobody expects you to know the words yet.

read.label: I'm a new Christian. What do I do now? The care page this plan walks beside

tool.label: The Theological Vocabulary Glossary, one hundred church words, each explained first in a single sentence

weeks.reflection: What actually happened to me, in my own words, with no borrowed language?

weeks.focus: Reading Mark, a chapter a day
weeks.why: The Bible is a library, and you don't have to start at page one. Begin with Mark, the shortest of the four Gospels, the accounts of Jesus' life: sixteen chapters, a little over two weeks at a chapter a day. Read to meet the person at the center. Mark wastes no time. His first line names his subject, "This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God" (Mark 1:1), and gospel means good news. The rest of the book shows people struggling to see what the reader is told at the start. When you finish, read another Gospel and keep going.
weeks.practice: Read one chapter of Mark each day, slowly. Write down one line that stopped you and one question it raised, and keep the questions for a pastor or a friend. If you miss a day, pick up where you left off rather than doubling up.

read.label: How to Actually Read the Bible, a plain method that starts with Mark and asks three simple questions

tool.label: Mark 1 in the free Study Bible, where the reading begins, with notes on the chapter

weeks.reflection: What is Jesus actually like in Mark, and where does he surprise me?

weeks.why: Prayer is talking with God honestly, and there are no special words to learn first. Jesus' own disciples asked for help; one of them said, "Lord, teach us to pray" (Luke 11:1), so you're in good company. He answered with a pattern, the Lord's Prayer (Luke 11:2-4), which Matthew gives in the longer form most churches pray (Matthew 6:9-13), and you can pray it a line at a time, adding a sentence of your own after each. If Father is a hard word because of the father you had, or didn't have, you can still pray it; God is the Father no earthly father fully was. Short and honest prayers are welcome, and God isn't grading the grammar.
weeks.practice: Once a day, pray the Lord's Prayer slowly from Matthew 6:9-13, adding a sentence of your own after each line. At "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11), ask for what today needs. At "forgive us our debts" (Matthew 6:12), name what you've done wrong and anyone you need to forgive. On days when words won't come, praying it as written still counts.

read.label: The Lord's Prayer: A Bible Study Line by Line

tool.label: The Prayer Planner, for giving each person you pray for a day of the week

weeks.reflection: What do I keep editing out of my prayers, and who taught me God needed the edit?

weeks.focus: Finding a church, and asking about baptism
weeks.why: This faith was never meant to be lived alone. The first Christians "devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer" (Acts 2:42), and those four things are what to look for, not perfection; within a few chapters that same church faced a lie in its midst (Acts 5:1-11) and widows being overlooked (Acts 6:1). The people who believed that day were baptized (Acts 2:41), washed with water that marked them as belonging to Jesus, so ask about baptism early. Churches answer differently what baptism does, whom to baptize, and how. It's a question that divides churches, not the faith, so ask the church you visit what it teaches, and say so if you were baptized as a child.
weeks.practice: Pick one church to visit this Sunday, tell the pastor you're new, and ask what the church believes about baptism. Go at least three times before you decide. If you're unsure about Communion, the bread and cup Jesus gave his followers, it's fine to sit it out and ask. If a church or leader tells you to cut off your family, hand over your money, or stop asking questions, walk away.

read.label: Finding a Church, on looking for a faithful church rather than a perfect one

tool.label: What Does Baptism Mean, and Why Does It Matter? With the views of faithful Christians who differ

weeks.reflection: What am I most afraid of about belonging somewhere, and where did that fear come from?

weeks.focus: When the old self comes back
weeks.why: Before long, the temper or the habit you thought you'd left behind may turn up again, and you may wonder whether anything happened at all. Falling back doesn't prove nothing happened. It shows that sin, the wrong we do and the turning from God beneath it, has deep roots, in beginners and old saints alike. The first letter of John, written to believers, admits, "If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves" (1 John 1:8). God isn't waiting for you to clean up before he loves you; the love came first, and the change grows out of it, slowly. Many of us were handed a decision without an apprenticeship, or a rulebook before we could stand. Jesus' invitation is gentler: "Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me; for I am gentle and humble in heart" (Matthew 11:29).
weeks.practice: When you sin, tell God the truth the same day. Christians call this confession, and it comes with a promise: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). If the habit is drinking or drugs, tell a doctor, and if you drink or use every day, see one before you stop, because withdrawal can be dangerous; SAMHSA's helpline on Find Help can point you to treatment. If you came to faith during treatment, don't quit it because you feel strong.

read.label: How to Confess Sin and Walk in Repentance, on receiving forgiveness as finished

tool.label: Assurance of Faith, on resting in Christ's promise rather than in how strong your faith feels

weeks.reflection: Which part of my old life keeps coming back, and what do I believe God thinks of me when it does?

weeks.why: Questions you can't answer will come, sometimes in the first months, and a doubt doesn't mean the whole thing was fake. When the risen Jesus met his disciples on a mountain in Galilee, "they worshiped Him, but some doubted" (Matthew 28:17), and he sent them all anyway. A skeptic would say that what you felt has ordinary causes and will fade. Feelings do rise and fall, and the question is fair to ask, but the faith rests on what happened, not on how you feel tonight. Scripture is full of people who asked God hard questions to his face, and their questions were kept in the book. Bring yours into the open instead of carrying them alone.
weeks.practice: Start a notebook for questions. When one comes, write it down instead of pushing it away, and once this week ask one of them out loud to a pastor or a Christian friend. You don't have to answer them all now. If fear that you aren't really saved is filling hours of your day and no reassurance lasts, tell a pastor this week, and see a doctor or licensed counselor too.

read.label: I'm not sure I believe anymore, the care page for heavier questions

tool.label: Matthew 28 in the Study Bible, where some doubted and all were sent

weeks.reflection: What question am I most afraid to ask out loud, and what do I think would happen if I asked it?

weeks.focus: One friend, and your own story
weeks.why: Faith is learned the way a trade is learned, beside someone further along. Ask one Christian you trust, someone honest about their own faults, to walk with you for a month, and be wary of anyone who wants to run your decisions. Sooner or later, someone who knew you before will also notice something and ask, and you don't need a script or an answer for every objection. You have news about your own life. The man Jesus healed in John 9 couldn't answer every question the authorities put to him, but he could say, "There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see" (John 9:25).
weeks.practice: Ask one Christian you trust to meet weekly for a month, read the same chapter of Mark, trade questions, and pray for five minutes; if you're a teenager, meet at church or somewhere public. Then tell one person what happened to you, in your own words. If anyone at home threatens or hurts you because of your faith, your safety comes first: call 911 if you're in danger, and if you're under eighteen, tell a teacher or another adult you trust.

read.label: How to Tell Your Story, plainly and humbly, with no performance

tool.label: New Believers: A Study on Your First Steps of Faith, five sessions to work through with a friend

weeks.reflection: Who could walk with me for the next month, and who in my life would actually want to hear what happened to me?

weeks.focus: A rule small enough to keep
weeks.why: These eight weeks were a start, not a test, and there was no way to fail them. What carries a faith across years is rarely intensity; it's a few small practices kept in ordinary weeks, with other people. Christians call that a rule of life, a short written pattern of practices. It works like a trellis, a few chosen supports that hold a growing life up. Build yours small enough to keep on your worst week. And when the feeling fades, as feelings do, remember what Paul told a church he loved: "He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion" (Philippians 1:6).
weeks.practice: Write on one card the two or three practices from these weeks that helped, such as a chapter a day, the Lord's Prayer, Sunday with your church, or a weekly friend, and when you'll keep them. Show the card to the friend from last week and ask them to check on you. When you finish Mark, choose a reading plan from the plans page and keep going.

read.label: Spiritual Growth, on trading the search for a breakthrough for small practices kept over years

tool.label: The Rule of Life Builder, to choose a few rhythms and write them down

weeks.reflection: A year from now, what do I hope is ordinary in my life that is brand new today?
